articles.title: Rubio Trip Highlights US Push For Deeper Ties With Central Asia
articles.summary: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio departed Uzbekistan on October 20 for India after meetings with all five Central Asian countries, wrapping up a visit aimed at expanding Washington’s economic and diplomatic engagement with a region increasingly intent on shaping its own international partnerships.

articles.title: As Russian Arms Exports Slide, Central Asia Shops Elsewhere
articles.summary: Central Asian nations are increasingly turning to India, China, Turkey, and Europe for military equipment to reduce their dependence on Russia. articles.summary: The deportation of several Tajik opposition figures from Germany and other European countries, and their subsequent imprisonment, have heightened fears among Tajik oppositionists in exile. Some say they fear not only being sent home but also losing the Western support they once counted on.

articles.summary: Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha said that US President Donald Trump's decision to waive sweeping sanctions against Russia was "indecisiveness," which "sends the wrong message to the aggressor."

articles.title: Cold Play: Nations Line Up To Boycott Ice Hockey Games Against Russia
articles.summary: A growing list of countries are lining up against a court decision allowing Russia to rejoin international ice hockey events, saying they will boycott any team Moscow sends, putting the World Championships next year in jeopardy.

articles.title: Ukraine Monitoring 8 Tankers Carrying Russian Diesel Potentially Bound For US
articles.summary: Ukrainian authorities are monitoring eight tankers carrying more than 300,000 tons of Russian diesel fuel that could be bound for the United States, Ukrainian government sources told RFE/RL on November 3.

articles.title: Midterm Democrat Gains Likely To Put Trump's Russia, Ukraine, Iran Policies Under Pressure
articles.summary: Democratic Party victories in the US midterm elections are set to shift the balance of power in Congress, giving the party greater oversight and influence over legislation, with implications for US policy toward Russia, Ukraine, and Iran.

articles.title: Following Oleshky Truce, Melania Trump To Host Russia-Ukraine Talks
articles.summary: US first lady Melania Trump will host Russian and Ukrainian representatives at the White House on November 5 for a meeting following a localized cease-fire in Ukraine's southern Kherson region, as a new round of US-mediated peace talks is set to take place next week.

articles.title: Clashes Near Kyiv Highlight Tension Over Military Manpower Challenges
articles.summary: Crowds clashed with Ukrainian riot police and national guardsmen in a Kyiv suburb on November 2 in the latest tensions over military efforts to catch alleged deserters and enlist men -- sometimes forcibly -- to fight in the war against Russia.

articles.title: Ukrainian Crowd Clashes With Riot Police, Again Highlighting Recruitment Tactics, Military Morale
articles.summary: A crowd clashed with police and National Guard troops in a Kyiv suburb amid allegations that men were being held and tortured in a private house. The incident highlights growing tensions over Ukraine’s controversial military recruitment practices as it strives to repel Russia’s full-scale invasion.

articles.title: US, Russia, Ukraine To Resume Peace Talks Amid Doubts Over Breakthrough
articles.summary: The United States says it will host new Russia-Ukraine peace talks in Abu Dhabi on November 10-11, but analysts caution that deep divisions over a cease-fire and security guarantees make a major breakthrough unlikely.

articles.title: Trump Says Iran Wants A Deal 'And It Could Happen'
articles.summary: President Donald Trump repeated his assertion that the United States is winning the war with Iran and said that Tehran wants a deal, adding: “It could happen.”

articles.title: US Strikes Iranian Island As Trump Downplays Prospect Of Renewed Conflict
articles.summary: The United States has struck Iran’s strategic Qeshm Island in a series of previously undisclosed attacks. The strike, conducted on the eve of the US midterm elections, was carried out even as President Donald Trump played down the prospect of renewed war and signals hope for a diplomatic deal.

articles.title: Taliban Concerned Amid Reports Of US Deportation Of Afghans Via Pakistan
articles.summary: Afghanistan has asked the US government to “act responsibly” amid reports that it plans to deport dozens of Afghans via Pakistan, possibly in the coming days.

articles.title: Arrests, Resignations, Repainting: Here's What's Happening In Postelection Serbia
articles.summary: Events have moved fast since Student List won Serbia’s parliamentary elections on October 25. Here are some of the notable happenings that have unfolded in the week since former President Aleksandar Vucic was ousted from office after more than a decade in power.

articles.title: After A Crushing Defeat, What Now For Serbia's Vucic?
articles.summary: Former longstanding Serbian leader Aleksandar Vucic has said he’ll “come back” after losing elections in October. But is his future more likely to be in a court dock instead of the court of public opinion?

articles.title: Russian Strikes Kill More Than 30 In Ukrainian Town As Aid Hub Hit Multiple Times, Kyiv Says
articles.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said his country would cease strikes on Russian oil refineries – as demanded by US President Donald Trump -- if the US would provide Kyiv with Patriot air-defense missiles.

articles.title: 'We Escaped Hell': Oleshky Residents Reach Ukraine After Years In War-Torn City
articles.summary: Shaking with joy, relatives of Ukrainians who have endured years under Russian occupation with almost no food, water, or electricity rushed to greet their loved ones in tears in Chernihiv on October 31.

articles.title: 'Every Day Gets Harder': Victim's Family Speaks 2 Years After Serbia's Novi Sad Station Collapse
articles.summary: On November 1, 2024, 20-year-old Andjela Ruman arrived by train in Novi Sad, where her boyfriend was waiting for her. They died together when the station canopy collapsed. Two years on, her parents, Zorica and Zlatko Ruman, speak to RFE/RL about how they have been coping with their loss.

articles.title: Moscow Reports Drone Attack On Nizhny Novgorod As Russian Strikes Cut Power In Ukraine
articles.summary: Moscow and Kyiv traded strikes on November 1, with dozens of drones reportedly destroyed over Russia's Nizhny Novgorod region and energy infrastructure hit in four Ukrainian regions, leaving hundreds of thousands without power.

articles.title: Belarus Holding At Least 22 Political Prisoners In Psychiatric Hospitals, Rights Groups Say
articles.summary: At least 22 people in Belarus recognized as political prisoners by rights defenders face indefinite confinement inside secretive psychiatric hospitals. Cut off from amnesties and pardons, rights defenders warn that these individuals have effectively vanished into a legal "black zone."

articles.title: China, Russia Deepen Arctic Cooperation In Challenge To US
articles.summary: The 31st meeting of the Chinese and Russian heads of government held in St. Petersburg on October 21 was notable for its focus on cooperation in the Arctic, where Beijing and Moscow are increasingly challenging the United States and its allies.

articles.title: Rubio Casts Doubts On Quick Deal To End War In Ukraine, Defends Russian Contacts
articles.summary: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he was unsure whether a negotiated end to the war in Ukraine was possible, while European officials told RFE/RL the top US diplomat privately expressed doubts that Russian President Vladimir Putin will attend December’s Miami G20 summit.

She is the founder of the Baloch Yakjehti Committee, a network of activists dedicated to peaceful advocacy for Pakistan’s Baloch minority, and she regularly organizes demonstrations and events to highlight the enforced disappearance, torture, and killing of Baloch people.

In a letter addressed to the United Nations, detained Karakalpak lawyer and journalist Dauletmurat Tazhimuratov writes, “In the 21st century, I am being held in a cell without a proper floor. It has been 60 days since I last had access to a bathhouse; I wash myself in the toilet.” HRF calls for Uzbekistan to release Dauletmurat Tazhimuratov, echoing his plea: “I beg you to help me and protect a man who, having already been knocked down, is still being beaten.” Learn more . https://kloop.kg/blog/2026/11/04/koroli-.body: Facebook Twitter VK Telegram WhatsApp Мост по улице Ауэзова, часть улиц Байтик Баатыра и Ахунбаева недавно пережили капремонт. Бишкек потратил на но это как минимум 740 млн сомов. Но новый асфальт быстро поплыл и просел, а власти на жалобы не реагируют. «Клооп» выяснил : двое из трех подрядчиков ремонта связаны с бывшим и действующими чиновниками. После капитального ремонта моста по улице Ауэзова, а также улиц Байтик Баатыра и Ахунбаева на новом асфальте появились колеи и трещины, а в некоторых местах дорожное покрытие и вовсе просело. Это снял на видео вице-спикер Жогорку Кенеша Болот Ибрагимов, который заявил, что новый асфальт «похож на пластилин» и «выглядит отвратительно». Ибрагимов потребовал провести независимое расследование капремонта с участием экспертов «международного уровня». Мост раздора Айбек Джунушалиев, мэр города Бишкек. Реконструкция моста по улице Ауэзова и ремонт дороги на нем начались в конце июня прошлого года. В ноябре 2025 года мэр Бишкека Айбек Джунушалиев торжественно открыл движение по мосту. По словам мэра, работы обошлись в 144 млн сомов — сумма, по его словам, оказалась настолько небольшой, что подрядчики не хотели браться за ремонт. Согласились только китайские инвесторы, при этом мэрия будет выплачивать деньги в рассрочку в течение трех лет. Сейчас те же китайские инвесторы строят в Бишкеке еще один мост. Мост по улице Ауэзова. Фото: Кактус Отвечая на критику Ибрагимова о некачественном асфальте на мосту по улице Ауэзова, мэр Бишкека Айбек Джунушалиев заявил, что на дорожное покрытие на это участке повлияла «интенсивность использования дороги». «Вот мост по Ауэзова. Вы просто в вечернее время посмотрите, сколько грузовой техники там проедет за час. И мы не оправдываемся. Мы выставили ряд требований — если они [подрядчики] сделают некачественно дорогу, то в течение трех лет они восстановят ее за свой счет. И мы это будем требовать и отстаивать», — сказал он . Король асфальта с российским паспортом А вот улицы Байтик Баатыра и Ахунбаева , которые также упомянул в своем видео Болот Ибрагимов, ремонтировали кыргызстанские компании. На их реконструкцию потратили куда более внушительные средства — почти 600 млн сомов за 8,6 км дорожного полотна. Журналисты «Клоопа» выяснили кто, стоит за компаниями, которые занимались строительством. Улица Байтик Баатыра. Фото: Кактус Отрезок дороги на Байтик Баатыра в 6,2 км ремонтировала компания «Технотоп» . В 2024 году мэрия Бишкека выделила на это почти 414 млн сомов: километр дороги обошелся городскому бюджету почти в 67 млн. Один из трех учредителей «Технотопа» — Горбунов Анатолий Анатольевич. С 2016 по 2021 годы он был депутатом Бишкекского горкенеша от партии «Республика — Ата-Журт». В 2020 году в медиа появилась информация, что у Горбунова есть российское гражданство — депутатам в Кыргызстане иметь двойное гражданство запрещено. Но городской избирком тогда это проверить не смог, и причина была очень странной: Горбунов не дал на это свое разрешение. Скрин: Кто есть кто Российский паспорт у Горбунова действительно тогда был, убедился «Клооп». Он получил его еще в 2011 году, свидетельствуют утечки российских баз данных. Но сейчас документ уже недействителен (возможно, срок действия документа просто закончился в 2021 году, когда Горбунову исполнилось 45 лет). Однако это не значит, что российского гражданства у экс-депутата больше нет. Официальным учредителем «Технотопа» во время своего депутатства Горбунов не был, но журналисты и тогда связывали его с компанией. Издание Kaktus.Media также писало, что тендеры от властей Бишкека выигрывала и другая фирма Горбунова — « Эксперт мастер строй» . «Технотоп» не впервые упоминается в скандальных новостях. В 2025 году во время ремонта улицы Шабдана Баатыра строители бросили на дороге бетонный блок без предупреждающих знаков. Из-за этого водитель грузовика «Хово», пытаясь увернуться от блока, смял легковушку, и ее водитель попал в больницу. Компанию тогда оштрафовали, но всего на 75 тысяч сомов. Кроме улиц Байтик Баатыра и Шабдан Баатыра, в течение последних трех лет «Технотоп» реконструировал или ремонтирует еще как минимум 15 улиц Бишкека . Также компания проложила асфальт на Площади Ала-Тоо и в аэропорту «Манас». А в 2022 году «Технотоп» уложила асфальт в природном парке «Ала-Арча». «Оказывается они слабые » Улица Ахунбаева. Скрин: Акипресс Улицу Ахунбаева, о которой также на видео говорил Болот Ибрагимов, в 2024 году ремонтировала компания «ДорСтрой Групп» . На капремонт 2,4 км дороги город выделил 182,2 млн сомов — по 79 млн за километр . Но даже эту пару километров они не смогли построить сами. Летом 2024 года инспекция во главе с премьер-министром Акылбеком Жапаровым выяснила , что у «ДорСтрой Групп» не хватает техники. Но вместо того, чтобы нанять другого подрядчика, власти лишь слегка пожурили компанию — и дали ей городскую технику. «Оказывается они слабые. Слабоватые, мы даем [им] свою технику от “Бишкекасфальтсервиса”. И говорим, что [...] если не уложатся в срок, не захотят брать технику и будут делать самостоятельно, то мы грозим им, что включим их в черный список», — говорил тогда мэр Айбек Джунушалиев. Асфальт уложили некачественно — спустя некоторое время после окончания капремонта улицы Ахунбаева компания «ДорСтрой Групп» восстанавливала недавно проложенное дорожное покрытие по трехлетней гарантии на восстановление дефектов. Тогда же из-за постоянных жалоб на некачественную реконструкцию дорог, обратил внимание на проблему и ГКНБ. Среди дорог, которые быстро пришли в негодность после капремонта, была и улица Ахунбаева, отремонтированная «ДорСтрой Групп». Тогда ГКНБ признал нарушения и сообщил о доследственной проверке. Но ее итоги до сих пор неизвестны. Но это не помешало компании получить подряд на продолжение реконструкции улицы Ахунбаева в 2026 году. Компания должна построить дорогу на отрезке улицы Ахунбаева от Достоевского до Ауэзова, со строительством моста через улицу Валиханова к Южному большому Чуйскому каналу. Также компания отвечает за ремонт еще не менее 9 улиц столицы . Управделами президента Каныбек Туманбаев. Фото: 24 Кроме того, «Дорстрой групп» осуществляет проекты, строительство которых курирует Управление делами президента. Это подъезды к новому Ошскому рынку и к новому Западному автовокзалу , а также дорога вокруг стадиона «Бишкек арена». А в 2023 году «ДорСтрой Групп» благоустраивала сквер в 2,4 га в жилом массиве Ак-Орго Бишкека за 87,2 млн сомов. По плану компания должна была озеленить территорию, пробурить скважину, проложить тротуары, построить туалеты, а также обустроить детские и игровые площадки. Однако результат оказался далёк от ожиданий: даже после благоустройства сквер выглядел неприглядно. парк в ж\м Ак-Өргө, фото Клооп Итак, кто же контролирует эту фирму? По видимому, это семейная компания Абдиласизовых. Айбек Абдиласизов, фото из соцсетей До 2021 года ее учредителем и директором был Абдиласизов Айбек Абдиласизович, который основал ее в 2014 году. Потом он передал владение компанией Абдиласизовой Асель Тынарбековне. А как минимум на декабрь 2024 коммерческим директором в ней был Абдиласизов Алишер Абдиласизович. Алишер Абдиласизов называет себя руководителем нового рынка «Ала-Тоо» (рядом с рынком «Мадина»). Владелец рынка — компания «Ордо Курулуш Компани» Козуева Алтынбека Уркунбаевича. Абдиласизов Айбек Абдиласизович « Владелец рынка — Козуев Алтынбек Уркунбаевич. Я — представитель этого человека», — говорил Алишер Абдилазизов на встрече с торговцами на новом рынке «Ала-Тоо». Козуев — уже довольно известная личность. В 2024 году журналисты OCCRP, Temirov Live и «Клоопа» выяснили , что он близок к управляющему делами президента Каныбеку Туманбаеву. Учредитель компании «Иншаат Строй Билдинг» Алтынбек Козуев и президент Кыргызстана Садыр Жапаров Примечательно, что «ДорСтрой Групп» участвовала в сносе гостиницы «Иссык-Куль» и в строительстве на ее месте нового здания администрации президента. https://www.rferl.org/a/tigers-kazakhsta.body: Kazakhstan 'Anti-Conflict' Teams Dispatched As Wild Tigers Return To Kazakhstan November 03, 2026 16:56 CET By Amos Chapple Photo: Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources of the Republic of Kazakhstan (Courtesy Image) Kazakhstan 'Anti-Conflict' Teams Dispatched As Wild Tigers Return To Kazakhstan November 03, 2026 16:56 CET By Amos Chapple 'Anti-Conflict' Teams Dispatched As Wild Tigers Return To Kazakhstan Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Two tigers are now prowling the Kazakh wilderness, nearly 80 years after the last spotting of the apex predators in the country. On November 2, Kazakhstan's Ecology and Natural Resources Ministry announced the release of a male tiger named Amur into a nature reserve set up to host the big cats. Amur will share the Ile-Balkhash State Nature Reserve, some 300 kilometers northwest of Almaty, with a female tiger from Russia called Umit who was loosed into the same reserve on July 31. Within 10 days of her historic release, the female had killed and eaten a boar and a wolf and has reportedly adapted to life in the Kazakh wilderness successfully. Umit, the first tiger to be released into the Ile-Balkhash State Nature Reserve, walks through marshes moments after her release on July 31. Valery Bilyachenko runs a recreational fishing base near where the tigers were released and is one of those in the area keeping a close eye on how the project develops. He told RFE/RL locals are largely opposed to the tiger reintroduction project. "The main livelihood in the local villages is livestock farming," he pointed out. "There are pastures and cattle, and naturally, local people are worried that the tigers will kill their animals." Some villages are located just tens of kilometers from where the two tigers were released. "The tigers are now fitted with satellite-tracking collars, so their movements are being monitored, and we've been told that when the tigers begin approaching villages, special teams will be sent out to scare them away," Bilyachenko said. Kazakhstan has vowed to maintain roaming "anti-conflict" teams to prevent incidents between tigers and humans or livestock. Additionally, automated texts will reportedly alert locals whenever a tiger roams within 5 kilometers of a village or farm. Male tiger Amur was released into the Kazakh reserve on October 31. "Our main goal is not simply to return these predators to their historic range but to establish a stable population capable of living and breeding independently in the wild," Kazakh Ecology and Natural Resources Ministry Alibek Kuantyrov said after Amur's release. It is hoped the two tigers currently loose in the reserve will eventually find each other and have a "tiger wedding," though experts say the chances of the pair mating are small. For his fishing lodge business, Bilyachenko says he predicts little impact in the near term, though that may change. Two more young tigers are set to be released into the reserve in 2027, and the eventual aim is for around 50 big cats roaming the wilderness of Kazakhstan, opening the prospect of tiger-spotting tourism but potentially limiting people's willingness to freely enjoy the outdoors in the area. A file photo of kulans running grassland in Kazakhstan The Ile-Balkhash State Nature Reserve was established in 2018 and has been prepared specifically for tigers through the introduction of more than 200 deer and over 100 kulans, a donkey-like animal native to Central Asia that will supplement the "prey base" of the big cats. The $30 million tiger project is a joint effort between Kazakhstan and Russia -- where the animals are sourced from -- and has been funded by the World Wildlife Fund, UNDP, and Kazakhstan. Hunters carry a tiger in the far east of Siberia in 1954. Kazakhstan was once home to a significant tiger population, but amid hunting and habitat destruction their number dwindled to an estimated 10 animals in the mid-1930s. By 1948, the big cats are believed to have disappeared completely from the territory of today's Kazakhstan. "This project sends a signal to the world. No country has ever restored a historically extinct species of large mammal, especially a predator," Sergey Aramilev, the director-general of Russia's Amur Tiger Center, said of the Kazakh project . If the initiative proves successful, he says, the reintroduction of the animals "will show other countries that it is possible." https://www.rferl.org/a/ukraine-tankers-.body: News Ukraine Monitoring 8 Tankers Carrying Russian Diesel Potentially Bound For US By Alex Raufoglu November 04, 2026 08:47 CET Ukraine Monitoring 8 Tankers Carrying Russian Diesel Potentially Bound For US Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google The Agioi Fanendes (pictured in 2024) is believed to be carrying about 40,000 tonnes of Russian ultra-low-sulfur diesel, but its discharge port remains unknown. WASHINGTON -- Ukrainian authorities are monitoring eight tankers carrying more than 300,000 tons of Russian diesel fuel that could be bound for the United States, Ukrainian government sources told RFE/RL on November 3. Seven of the vessels have declared the United States as their destination, while the eighth, the Greek-flagged Athina M., is suspected of making a similar voyage. Four tankers -- Leruo, Primorye, Manta, and Feliks -- are subject to European Union, British, and Ukrainian sanctions, according to Ukrainian monitoring data, the sources said. They spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to comment publicly. On October 9, the US Treasury Department announced a temporary general license authorizing transactions related to the supply of Russian diesel to global markets in an attempt to ease price pressures. US President Donald Trump said he had agreed with his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin to release millions of tons of Russian diesel over three months for use in the United States and global markets. The vessels named by the Ukrainian sources loaded their cargoes at Russian ports in October, primarily at Primorsk on the Baltic Sea. Their estimated arrival dates to the United States range from November 7 to November 18. US Groups Track 13 Ships Two US-based advocacy organizations, the American Coalition for Ukraine and Razom for Ukraine, confirmed they are tracking 13 vessels that could deliver Russian diesel to US ports this week. The groups identified the Taurus and Agioi Fanendes as the two ships most likely to be carrying Russian fuel. The Taurus reportedly carries Russian diesel, although no cargo manifest has confirmed its contents. It stopped near the Port of Wilmington, North Carolina, on November 1, before returning to sea the following day. There is no evidence it unloaded cargo. SEE ALSO: Midterm Democrat Gains Likely To Put Trump's Russia, Ukraine, Iran Policies Under Pressure The Agioi Fanendes is believed to carry about 40,000 tons of Russian ultra-low-sulfur diesel, but its discharge port remains unknown. The groups said they had identified no US buyer or terminal. The Ukrainian government sources, speaking on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to comment publicly, put its cargo at 35,700 tons and said it was sailing west through the Atlantic, with an estimated arrival date of November 7. The advocacy groups said they were also tracking 11 additional vessels based on reported cargoes or their positions, adding that the number could increase. Experts Warn Of Legal Risks Eugene Goncharov, policy director at the American Coalition for Ukraine, told RFE/RL that importing Russian diesel would make little economic sense for the United States while providing revenue to Moscow. "The diesel deal is absurd in every sense of the word," Goncharov said, arguing the shipments would not lower prices for American consumers. He also noted the United States is itself a diesel exporter. "We're very concerned about the precedent it sets," he said, adding he welcomed efforts by Representatives Brian Fitzpatrick and Gregory Meeks to close loopholes in existing legislation. John Herbst, a former US ambassador to Ukraine and now a senior director at the Atlantic Council's Eurasia Center, said he believed the shipments would probably reach the United States unless a new obstacle emerged. SEE ALSO: Following Oleshky Truce, Melania Trump To Host Russia-Ukraine Talks "This is a deal Trump has already engineered," Herbst told RFE/RL. "Barring some new obstacle to the delivery of that diesel, I think it will be delivered.” However, he said, potential buyers could face legal consequences under the 2022 legislation banning Russian energy imports. Herbst cited warnings from US Senator Richard Blumenthal and said companies considering purchasing the fuel would have to weigh the possibility of legal action, even if the administration had authorized the transactions. New Jersey Warns Ports New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill has warned port officials and terminal operators that accepting Russian diesel could violate federal law and expose them to civil and criminal penalties. In a November 2 letter , Sherrill said neither Trump nor Treasury Department officials had blanket authority to waive the congressional ban on Russian energy imports, adopted in April 2022 following Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. She pledged to use legal and regulatory measures to prevent New Jersey ports from receiving the fuel. "New Jersey will not stand by while Donald Trump supports Vladimir Putin at the expense of Americans," Sherrill said in a statement, urging operators to turn away tankers carrying Russian fuel. SEE ALSO: The US Once Called It 'A Slush Fund For Putin.' Now Washington May Lift Sanctions On It Dispute Over US Authorization The controversy centers on the relationship between the 2022 Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act and Treasury's General License 135, which authorizes transactions involving Russian-origin diesel, including its importation into the United States, through April 7, 2027. The 2022 law prohibits Russian energy imports and allows the ban to be lifted only if the president certifies Russia has agreed to withdraw its forces and cease hostilities in Ukraine. Any termination is subject to a 90-day waiting period during which Congress can block it. Lawmakers from both parties have questioned whether the Treasury authorization conflicts with the congressional ban. A bipartisan group of senators, including Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski, Thom Tillis, and John Curtis, has said the imports violate the law. Tillis said Trump "may be" breaking the ban. The Trump administration has defended the authorization. A White House spokeswoman said the arrangement was intended to increase supply and lower fuel prices for American consumers. SEE ALSO: Russia's Poorer Regions Facing Brunt Of Health-Care Cuts As Military Spending Soars Herbst said allowing Russian diesel into the US market would undermine Washington's broader interests in Ukraine. "This is a serious policy mistake because our interests, American true interests, are making sure that Putin's aggression in Ukraine fails, and this makes it easier for Putin to continue that aggression," he told RFE/RL. He added that the controversy was deepening doubts in Kyiv and European capitals about Washington's reliability as a security partner. "There are doubts not just in Kyiv but in other European capitals about the reliability of the United States to perform as it has since the end of World War II," he said. Oil and gas revenues are a major source of funding for the Kremlin. Russia's 2026 budget projected approximately 8.92 trillion rubles ($125 billion) in such revenue, according to figures cited by the advocacy groups. https://www.rferl.org/a/russia-hockey-uk.body: News Cold Play: Nations Line Up To Boycott Ice Hockey Games Against Russia By RFE/RL's Ukrainian Service November 04, 2026 14:25 CET Cold Play: Nations Line Up To Boycott Ice Hockey Games Against Russia Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Many of ice hockey's most-powerful nations are lining up to boycott a court decision reinstating Russia to the international arena. (file photo) A growing list of countries are lining up against a court decision allowing Russia to rejoin international ice hockey events, saying they will boycott any team Moscow sends, putting the World Championships next year in jeopardy. A major hockey power, Russia has been banned from global competition by the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. SEE ALSO: International Bans On Russian Sports, Entertainment Pile Up But on October 30, the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruled the federation must reinstate Russian teams beginning with next month's World Junior Hockey Championships in Canada. The IIHF said it disagreed with the ruling but would comply. The decision has sparked sharp criticism from Ukraine and many of the world's hockey powers who support Kyiv, which says the court ruling was "staining the ice with Ukrainian blood" and urging its partners to take a "firm stand" against Russia's return. "Russia and Belarus are supporting this illegal, unjustified, horrific war in Ukraine. As long as that's going on, there will be none of those athletes competing for their countries in Canada," Prime Minister Mark Carney said on November 3. Carney's announcement is especially key since Canada will host the World Junior championships less than two months, which would have been the first major tournament with Russian participation since the 2022 Beijing Olympics. The Kremlin launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine just days after the Games ended. At least six European nations, including prominent hockey countries Sweden, the Czech Republic, Norway, Denmark, Latvia, and Finland, the reigning men's world champions, have said they will refuse to play against Russia despite the ruling. The German hockey federation, which is to host the 2027 World Championships in May, has said the ruling “fundamentally changes the situation” for it as host nation. "Allowing Russia to participate would have serious consequences for us as the host country in terms of security, as well as politically and economically," according to German ice hockey federation (DEB) Chairman Frank Lutz, adding the DEB was analyzing how it will proceed. "Our position remains unchanged: we reject the return of Russian national teams to international ice hockey tournaments," Lutz said. A number of longtime sponsors of the men's world championship, including Swedish furniture company AJ Products and Czech carmaker Skoda Auto, have already vowed to reassess their involvement in the tournament if Russia's team is reinstated. The CAS ruling also sent a shockwave across Ukraine when it was handed down. Ukrainian authorities had often noted that hundreds of the country's athletes had been killed in Russia's war and hundreds of sports facilities were damaged or destroyed by Moscow's relentless air attacks. SEE ALSO: Ukrainian Olympian Urges US To Bar Russian Athletes From 2028 Games The Ukrainian Ice Hockey Federation did not immediately respond for comment, but Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha said in a statement on social media on November 4 that "there is no impunity [for Russia] on ice." "Moscow still believes it can hide its crimes behind a hockey jersey and that an ice rink can restore its battered reputation," he said while applauding Canada's move and calling on more nations to join the boycott. Moscow appeared to downplay the wave of opposition to its return to the international hockey arena, with Sports Minister Mikhail Degtyarev saying that "the world is much bigger than Scandinavia or the Baltic states." In its ruling, CAS said that the IIHF's justifications for maintaining the ban on Russian teams, which included safety and security concerns, "were not supported by sufficient evidence." At the same time, it provided the federation with no guidance on how to reintegrate Russia after years of absence, during which the sport's landscape had significantly changed. Despite expressing "disappointment" with the move, the IIHF said on October 30 that it "will act in accordance" with it. It later added that "the global impact" of the CAS ruling had been "significantly underestimated." "The immediate reintegration of Russian teams presents significant practical and sporting challenges," the IIHF said on November 4, citing "visa and entry requirements, security provisions, logistical constraints and consequences for competition formats, all compounded by the limited time available, with some events only weeks away." The CAS ruling does not apply to the Women's World Championships, which begin on November 6 in Denmark. Russia will not play in that tournament. Russian men have won five world championships and one Olympic gold medal since the country succeeded the Soviet Union in 1992. Soviet teams won 22 titles and seven gold medals before the country broke apart. https://www.rferl.org/a/ukraine-russia-o.body: News Following Oleshky Truce, Melania Trump To Host Russia-Ukraine Talks By Alex Raufoglu November 03, 2026 22:18 CET Following Oleshky Truce, Melania Trump To Host Russia-Ukraine Talks Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Evacuated residents of Oleshky greet their loved ones after arriving safely in Ukrainian-held territory in the Chernihiv region on October 31. WASHINGTON -- US first lady Melania Trump will host Russian and Ukrainian representatives at the White House on November 5, with both sides confirming their participation in a meeting following a localized cease-fire in Ukraine's southern Kherson region, as a new round of US-mediated peace talks is set to take place next week. The meeting follows a six-day cease-fire in and around the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky, which Melania Trump said she helped broker to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and the evacuation of vulnerable civilians. According to sources who spoke to RFE/RL, Ukraine will be represented by David Arakhamia, head of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's Servant of the People parliamentary faction, and Dmytro Lubinets, the country's human rights ombudsman. Russia is expected to send Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev, head of the Russian Direct Investment Fund, and Yana Lantratova, Russia's human rights commissioner. US First Lady Melania Trump (file photo) The announcement comes amid renewed diplomatic activity, with Russia confirming on November 3 that trilateral talks involving Moscow, Kyiv, and Washington will take place in Abu Dhabi on November 10-11. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said longtime Russian President Vladimir Putin aide Vladimir Medinsky would lead Moscow's delegation at the talks in the UAE. The discussions, mediated by Washington, are expected to address efforts to end Russia's nearly five-year full-scale war against Ukraine, postwar security arrangements, and ways to de-escalate the conflict. Oleshky Cease-Fire Offers Humanitarian Breakthrough The localized cease-fire around Oleshky from October 27 to November 2 was intended to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and the evacuation of vulnerable civilians. Melania Trump announced on October 23 that she had helped secure the arrangement after raising the humanitarian situation in Oleshky with Russian and Ukrainian leadership. Her office said the initiative enabled the delivery of critical aid and the evacuation of nearly 800 people, who were able to return to Ukrainian-controlled territory. SEE ALSO: US, Russia, Ukraine To Resume Peace Talks Amid Doubts Over Breakthrough The humanitarian situation in Oleshky had become increasingly desperate. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha said in September that some residents had been forced to eat grass and weeds amid shortages of food, medicine, clean water, and electricity. The city, located on the eastern bank of the Dnieper River in the occupied Kherson region, had a prewar population of about 24,000. Only a fraction of its residents remained after displacement and evacuations. Ukraine, however, accused Russian forces of exploiting the temporary pause to reinforce their military positions in the area. Eugene Goncharov, director of policy at the American Coalition for Ukraine, said he welcomed the Oleshky cease-fire as evidence that Russia was capable of agreeing to localized pauses in fighting when it chose to do so, but cautioned against expecting a broader breakthrough. "We don't have high expectations," he told RFE/RL, arguing Russia could end the war at any time but had repeatedly chosen not to engage in serious cease-fire efforts. "The important thing to remember here is that Russia can at any point end this war and just chooses not to," he said. SEE ALSO: Russian Strikes Kill More Than 30 In Ukrainian Town As Aid Hub Hit Multiple Times, Kyiv Says Goncharov said he hoped the latest initiative would prove different, adding: "Perhaps this time will be different." As evacuations from the war-torn city continued on October 30, the Kremlin said the temporary cease-fire there should not be extrapolated to the broader peace settlement process in Ukraine. Moscow has repeatedly said it was not seeking a partial easing of the conflict, urging a complete resolution that would include its demands, including full control over Ukrainian territories that Russian forces have been unable to seize on the battlefield. Cautious Hopes For The Peace Process Matthew Boyse, a senior fellow at the Hudson Institute and a former deputy assistant secretary of state for European and Eurasian affairs during Donald Trump's first administration, said Russia could be seeking to build on the initiative by offering further localized cease-fires in return for major Ukrainian concessions. Although postwar security arrangements and de-escalation may feature in the upcoming discussions, Boyse said, the gap between Moscow and Kyiv remained too wide for an agreement to be within reach. "These issues may be on the agenda, but the sides have been so far apart on them that it is difficult to imagine how their differences can be bridged at this time," he told RFE/RL. He added that Russia believes time is on its side. The US and Ukraine support a cease-fire, Taylor said, but it remains unclear whether Moscow is prepared to do the same. "If the Russians agree to a ceasefire, that would be a breakthrough," he told RFE/RL. Taylor said that once a political agreement to stop fighting was reached, military experts could work out the technical details, including monitoring mechanisms using drones, surveillance aircraft and sensors, as well as procedures for dealing with violations. "That's easy," he said. "The hard part and the breakthrough would be for Putin to say yes, he's agreed to a cease-fire." Against this backdrop of cautious expectations, international efforts to advance the peace process are continuing. The European Commission is scheduled to host US, Ukrainian, and European representatives in Brussels on November 4. Delegations from France, Germany, Britain, and NATO will also attend, alongside the World Bank. Another gathering of the Coalition of the Willing, a group of Ukraine's closest allies working to support its defense against Russia's invasion, is scheduled for November 19. Meanwhile, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio is expected to attend a November 9-10 Group of Seven foreign ministers' meeting in Marseille, France, where Ukraine will be among the key issues. https://www.rferl.org/a/democrats-midter.body: News Analysis Midterm Democrat Gains Likely To Put Trump's Russia, Ukraine, Iran Policies Under Pressure By Alex Raufoglu November 04, 2026 06:43 CET Midterm Democrat Gains Likely To Put Trump's Russia, Ukraine, Iran Policies Under Pressure Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Midterm elections in the United States on November 3 saw the Democratic Party take control of Congress. WASHINGTON -- Democratic Party victories in the US midterm elections are set to shift the balance of power in Congress, giving the party greater oversight and influence over legislation, with implications for US policy toward Russia, Ukraine, and Iran. A wave of Democrat victories at voting booths across the country on November 3 is projected to wrest control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives from President Donald Trump's Republicans, according to projections by several major US news organizations. The results represent a significant shift in congressional power, giving Democrats greater influence over federal spending, administration oversight, and presidential nominations. SEE ALSO: US Strikes Iranian Island As Trump Downplays Prospect Of Renewed Conflict Trump said he was willing to accept the election results and work with Democrats, according to The New York Times. "We'll work with the Democrats, and we'll, you know, look forward to working with them. We'll probably work something out," Trump was quoted as saying. Trump retains broad authority over diplomacy and military operations, while Republican opposition and the president's veto power could limit efforts to translate Democratic victories into legislative changes. The election comes as the United States and Israel remain at war with Iran, Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine continues, and Washington's approach to Moscow remains a source of bipartisan disagreement. The most immediate foreign policy test for the incoming Congress may be the war with Iran. Democrats campaigned on ending the conflict, which has contributed to rising energy prices and economic uncertainty. Their control of both chambers will strengthen their ability to scrutinize the administration, challenge military spending, and push for limits on military operations. Dania Arayssi, program head and senior analyst at the New Lines Institute for Strategy and Policy, who regularly briefs congressional and executive branch decision-makers, told RFE/RL that the election results could push Trump toward a diplomatic exit from the war. "The outcomes of the election, particularly seeing the Democrats winning the House and the Senate, will definitely push the Trump administration to push for an exit strategy from the war, particularly through diplomatic tools and negotiations," she said. Arayssi said Democrats could block additional funding for the conflict and investigate the administration's decisions once the new Congress convenes in January. "This also means that the Iranians will not be under pressure to offer any additional compromise," she said. Many analysts also cautioned that despite the Democrats' landslide victory, the impact is far from predetermined. Trump remains commander-in-chief and retains considerable authority over military operations and diplomacy. Most Republicans have defended the Iran campaign as necessary to counter Iranian nuclear and regional threats and are likely to resist Democratic efforts to restrict funding. Nevertheless, the economic consequences of the conflict have become a political liability for the administration. Higher gasoline and diesel prices, partly linked to disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz, helped Democrats make affordability a central campaign issue. The incoming Congress could also intensify scrutiny of the Pentagon and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, while funding negotiations could create further confrontations with the White House. SEE ALSO: US, Russia, Ukraine To Resume Peace Talks Amid Doubts Over Breakthrough Meanwhile for Kyiv, which has relied on US support for more than four years in its battle to repel invading Russian forces, the results bring both uncertainty and reassurance. Several prominent congressional supporters of Ukraine are leaving office, including Republican Representative Don Bacon, a vocal critic of Russia who has frequently broken with his party and the White House over support for Kyiv. "I'm an old-school Reagan Republican and see the Russian invasion of Ukraine [as] the most important crisis facing the free world," Bacon told RFE/RL on November 3. "I hope we elect a 120th Congress that is stronger in its support for our friend and ally," he added. However, other departing Republican lawmakers include former Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell, Senators Thom Tillis, Bill Cassidy, and John Cornyn, as well as Representative Michael McCaul. Their departures remove several influential voices who have advocated a tougher approach toward Moscow. Nevertheless, Ukrainian-American organizations say they believe support for Kyiv will remain bipartisan. "While we are losing titan supporters of Ukraine in this election cycle, we are mindful of those who will remain and are encouraged on a bipartisan manner that Ukraine will still garner significant support," Michael Sawkiw, president of the Ukrainian Congress Committee of America, told RFE/RL. Sawkiw identified congressional oversight of the administration's recent waiver of Russia sanctions and its diesel deal, increased security assistance to Ukraine, and an extension of Temporary Protected Status for Ukrainian refugees as priorities. Dozens of buses carrying civilians left the war-torn town of Oleshky for the first time in more than four years on October 30, with people choosing whether to travel to Ukrainian- or Russian-controlled territory. https://cpj.org/2026/11/china-orders-jou.body: Share this: Share on Bluesky (Opens in new window) Bluesky Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Share on LinkedIn (Opens in new window) LinkedIn Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on WhatsApp (Opens in new window) WhatsApp Email a link to a friend (Opens in new window) Email New York, November 3, 2026 —The Committee to Protect Journalists calls on Chinese authorities to immediately release veteran journalist Dong Yuyu instead of ordering him to carry out prison labor weeks after lung surgery to remove a cancerous tumor. “It is inhumane of Chinese authorities to expect 64-year-old Dong Yuyu to resume prison labor weeks after major surgery and demonstrates a blatant disregard for his life,” said CPJ Asia-Pacific Director Beh Lih Yi. “Dong Yuyu should not even be in prison on a bogus espionage charge. Chinese authorities must halt all prison labor demands and release him on humanitarian grounds.” Dong, who is serving a seven-year sentence , was ordered to resume prison labour on October 12, working about 40 hours a week making clothes, just weeks after he underwent surgery in August at a prison hospital in the capital Beijing, his family told CPJ. His health had since declined, they said. The tumor was detected in May, after Dong was admitted to hospital with heart palpitations and weight loss. In March, Dong was transferred from Beijing No. 2 Prison, about 40 kilometers (25 miles) from the family’s Beijing home, to Chaobai Prison in the southeastern city of Tianjin, about 168 kilometers (104 miles) away, his family told CPJ. As a result, what was once a 40-minute drive to visit Dong now takes the family more than two hours. Dong, who was an editor and columnist at the state-owned Guangming Daily, was arrested in 2022 while having lunch with a Japanese diplomat in Beijing. He was convicted of espionage in November 2024 and sentenced to seven years in jail. CPJ has been advocating for Dong’s release and honored him with a 2025 International Press Freedom Award. China was the world’s worst jailer of journalists in CPJ’s 2025 prison census , with 49 currently behind bars. China’s foreign ministry did not immediately respond to a CPJ’s emailed request for comment. https://rsf.org/fr/enqu%C3%AAte-rsf-pres.body: Enquête RSF. Pressions, détentions et propagande : comment le Bureau 015 des renseignement talibans fait taire les journalistes et impose son narratif Organisation : RSF_fr Partager facebook twitter linkedin Courriel Torture, arrestations, condamnations arbitraires, fermetures de médias... Cinq ans après leur retour au pouvoir, les talibans poursuivent leur stratégie de musellement des journalistes. Au cœur de ce dispositif de surveillance et de répression de la presse, le redouté Bureau 015 des services de renseignement, aussi chargé de mener une guerre d’influence en ligne. Des reporters afghans ont accepté de livrer leur témoignage, certains pour la première fois et sous couvert d’anonymat pour des raisons de sécurité, auprès de Reporters sans frontières (RSF). “Un véritable dispositif de surveillance, d’intimidation et de répression a été mis en place par les talibans pour museler la presse afghane. Le Bureau 015 est au cœur de ce système, dans lequel les journalistes sont traités comme des ennemis du régime pour avoir simplement exercé leur métier. Arrestations arbitraires, menaces, interrogatoires, torture... : les témoignages recueillis par RSF décrivent des pratiques d’une extrême gravité, visant à instaurer un climat de censure, de terreur et à réduire les journalistes au silence. Autant de pratiques qui s’inscrivent dans une stratégie de répression totale du journalisme et qui confirment le statut de prédateur de la liberté de la presse 2026 du chef suprême des talibans, Haibatullah Akhundzada. Célia Mercier Responsable du bureau Asie du Sud de RSF La tête recouverte d’un sac en tissu noir, le journaliste Farhad*, arrêté quelques heures plus tôt, est conduit en voiture dans un bureau de la Direction générale du renseignement des talibans (GDI) dans la capitale, Kaboul. “Tu es un espion !” , lui lance un des agents. Son téléphone et son ordinateur sont passés au peigne fin. Son interrogatoire commence et les coups se mettent à pleuvoir. Car il a osé raconter la vie quotidienne de la population, on lui reproche de faire de la propagande contre l’Émirat islamique d’Afghanistan. Il fait partie des 77 journalistes arrêtés et détenus, depuis 2021, sur des périodes allant d’une semaine à deux ans, dans une vague d’arrestations massive pour terroriser les professionnels de l’information. Dans cette répression, un acteur joue un rôle majeur : le Bureau 015, où Farhad est transféré quelques jours après son arrestation. “Le Bureau 015 s’occupe uniquement des journalistes et surveille tous les médias” , décrit le reporter. Il y sera détenu deux semaines, enfermé dans une cellule minuscule : “J’étais seul, j’entendais parfois des voix. Mais je ne voyais pas d’autres prisonniers.” Différents bourreaux se relaient pour les interrogatoires. “C’est là que j’ai été le plus torturé. J’étais interrogé quand ils voulaient, jour et nuit. Ils me demandaient de dénoncer d’autres journalistes mais j’ai tenu bon. Ils m’ont asséné des coups très violents dans le dos, sur les pieds, ils ont aussi utilisé un pistolet à impulsion électrique . Aujourd’hui encore, je souffre des séquelles de ces tortures.” Le Bureau 015, tant redouté par les journalistes afghans, opère, sous l’égide de la GDI, le service des renseignements des talibans, depuis leur retour au pouvoir en août 2021. Le bureau dispose d’agents au siège de Kaboul et dans les provinces. Ceux-ci surveillent le contenu des médias afghans (radios, télévisions etc.) et signalent les éléments jugés problématiques. Ils convoquent les journalistes dont les reportages sont jugés critiques et les menacent. Via leur section des opérations, souvent en lien avec le ministère de la Promotion de la vertu et de la Prévention du vice, ils mènent des descentes dans les locaux des médias afghans, procèdent à des arrestations et des saisies de matériel. Cela a notamment été le cas pour la chaîne de télévision Tolonews , en mai 2026, ainsi que dans les bureaux de la Fédération des journalistes et des organisations de médias d'Afghanistan en juillet 2025 . " Nous allons te retrouver, où que tu sois, quel que soit l’endroit où tu te caches” Depuis leur retour au pouvoir, les talibans imposent une censure implacable. “Faire notre travail, c’était de fait, être contre les talibans”, résume Ahmad*, un journaliste interrogé par RSF. “Pendant les premières années, nous avons tenté de continuer d’exercer notre métier, mais nous étions en danger”. Il a dû quitter le pays depuis. Pour Ahmad, qui travaillait dans une chaîne de télévision, les pressions ont commencé, raconte-t-il, par l’interdiction d’émissions ou l’invisibilisation des femmes journalistes. Peu après le retour au pouvoir des talibans, le média a dû s’engager auprès du ministère de l’Information et de la Culture à “ne pas diffuser de programmes mixtes” et à “ne pas réaliser d’entretiens avec des personnes exprimant des opinions opposées au régime” . Progressivement, les menaces se font plus pesantes, avec des convocations régulières d’Ahmad au sein du Bureau 015 à la suite de sujets qui avaient déplu. Selon Abdul*, un autre journaliste en exil : “Ils veulent transformer les médias en organes de propagande au service du pouvoir, qui ne diffusent que les contenus qu’ils souhaitent.” RSF a recensé plus d’une vingtaine de directives nationales et une liste croissante d’arrêtés provinciaux visant à démanteler la liberté de la presse. Abdul, qui travaillait dans l’audiovisuel, raconte lui aussi avoir été menacé à plusieurs reprises lors de ces convocations au Bureau 015. “Ils me disaient : ‘Tu n’as pas besoin de faire des reportages sur les droits des femmes, les incidents sécuritaires, ou sur la pauvreté. Il faut que tu invites des personnes qui sont de notre côté et pas celles qui s’opposent aux intérêts nationaux !” , raconte le journaliste. Dans des messages audios que RSF a pu consulter, des membres du Bureau 015 menacent des journalistes à plusieurs reprises. Ils leur demandent de ne pas donner la parole à des personnes “provocatrices” qui “remettent en question la politique de l’Émirat islamique”, et ordonnent d’inviter des “analystes” choisis parmi une liste établie par les talibans - une liste ne dépassant pas une cinquantaine de personnes selon un journaliste. “Notre coopération doit être réciproque” , affirme l’un des agents, avant d’exiger la réalisation “de reportages et d’ interviews” sur des sujets souhaités par les talibans. Et même en exil, les menaces continuent, avec des messages de cet acabit : “Nous allons te retrouver, où que tu sois, quel que soit l’endroit où tu te caches.” Torture et simulacre d’exécution Un jour, Ahmad* est emmené de force au Bureau 015. Durant l’interrogatoire, il est accusé, comme d’autres, d’être un espion. “J’ai été torturé” , raconte-t-il, “les coups étaient si violents que j’ai fini par perdre connaissance”. Le journaliste est ensuite transféré dans une autre unité de la GDI. Le bureau 015 ne disposant pas de sa propre prison, la plupart des détenus sont ensuite transférés vers les départements 40 ou 90 de la GDI. Durant sa longue détention, il ne voit sa famille qu’à deux reprises et subit notamment un simulacre d’exécution. “À deux heures du matin, ils m’ont emmené sur une colline. Ils m’ont braqué une arme sur la tempe et m’ont dit qu’ici ils avaient tué plusieurs personnes comme moi”, raconte le journaliste. Il sera finalement jugé dans un tribunal et condamné à de la prison pour “propagande contre le régime”. Au bout de quelques mois, il est transféré à la tristement célèbre prison de Bagram, à une soixantaine de kilomètres au nord de Kaboul, où “les journalistes sont traités comme des criminels” . Là-bas, Ahmad* a toujours les mains et pieds attachés, même quand il doit se rendre aux toilettes. Il décrit également des punitions avec de l’eau froide. À sa sortie de prison, le journaliste fuit l’Afghanistan. Contacté par RSF au sujet de la répression menée par le bureau 015, Hamdullah Fitrat, un porte-parole des talibans, a répo

https://rsf.org/fr/%C3%A9thiopie-suspens.body: Éthiopie : suspension abusive de The Reporter, principal et plus ancien média indépendant du pays Organisation : RSF_fr Partager facebook twitter linkedin Courriel Le 2 novembre, l’Autorité éthiopienne des médias a suspendu pour une durée indéterminée le certificat d’enregistrement de The Reporter, plus ancien groupe de presse indépendant du pays. Reporters sans frontières (RSF) déplore une nouvelle décision aux contours flous et appelle l’Autorité éthiopienne des médias à revenir sur sa décision. Les journaux en anglais et en langue amharique ainsi que les plateformes numériques de The Reporter sont à l’arrêt. Dans un communiqué publié le 2 novembre, l’Autorité éthiopienne des médias (EMA) reproche au groupe de presse d’avoir diffusé des "informations qui ternissent l'image du pays et nuisent à la sécurité nationale" . Sans préciser dans la décision les contenus mis en cause, l’organe de régulation estime que plusieurs articles publiés vont “à l'encontre des intérêts nationaux de l'Éthiopie”, rattrapée par la guerre dans la province du Tigré, au nord du pays, depuis septembre 2026. Cette décision a créé la stupéfaction au sein du monde médiatique éthiopien. “J’ai dû vérifier l’information trois fois” , explique un journaliste éthiopien, qui souhaite garder l’anonymat. “Personne ne pensait que les autorités iraient jusqu’à les faire fermer” , ajoute-t-il. Et pour cause : fondé en 1995, The Reporter est le plus grand média privé du pays, employant plusieurs centaines de personnes. L’EMA n’a pas répondu aux sollicitations de RSF. “Les autorités éthiopiennes viennent de priver brutalement des centaines d’employés de leur travail et des millions de citoyens d’une source d’information indépendante. La suspension des activités du plus ancien groupe de presse indépendant du pays, pour des accusations floues liées à l’image du pays et à la sécurité nationale ne précisant pas les contenus visés, nuit gravement au pluralisme de l’information dans le pays. Les autorités ne peuvent instrumentaliser la sécurité nationale pour museler la presse. Nous demandons à l'organe de régulation de revenir immédiatement sur cette mesure abusive et de rétablir sans délai le droit de The Reporter à informer librement. Sadibou Marong Directeur du bureau Afrique subsaharienne de RSF L’Autorité éthiopienne des médias n’en est pas à son coup d’essai. En février 2026, elle avait révoqué le certificat d'enregistrement en ligne du média indépendant Addis Standard , toujours au nom d’allégations non étayées de violations de l'éthique journalistique et des intérêts nationaux. Une décision contestée en justice par le média indépendant, qui fait face, depuis début août, à une escalade des pressions et intimidations. https://www.osce.org/secretariat/669441.body: Press release OSCE Secretary General visits Minsk, underlines need to revitalize open and constructive dialogue to rebuild a more secure and stable region Date: 4 November 2026 Place: MINSK Source: OSCE Secretariat , OSCE Secretary General MINSK, 4 November 2026 – OSCE Secretary General Feridun H. Sinirlioğlu concluded his first official visit to the Republic of Belarus today. He met with Aleksandr Lukashenko, President of the Republic of Belarus, and Maxim Ryzhenkov, Minister of Foreign Affairs. In his meetings, he reaffirmed the OSCE’s central role as a platform for dialogue and diplomatic engagement across its vast geography and emphasized the Organization’s comprehensive approach to security. The Secretary General also took part in the Fourth Minsk International Conference on Eurasian Security, held under the theme “Navigating international disorder in the spirit of co-operation: Can we solve the Eurasian security puzzle?”. On the margins of the conference, he met with Sergey Lavrov, Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Russian Federation. He welcomed recent confidence-building measures, including those negotiated by Commissioner for Human Rights of the Russian Federation Yana Lantratova and Ukrainian Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights Dmytro Lubinets, and expressed hope that these steps could be built upon in the future and contribute to further progress on other urgent humanitarian issues. https://uzbekistan.osce.org/news/project.body: News News Item OSCE convenes regional workshop on combating trafficking in human beings and labour exploitation in tourism and hospitality supply chains in Central Asia Issued on: 4 November 2026 Issued by: OSCE Project Co-ordinator in Uzbekistan , Office of the Special Representative and Co-ordinator for Combating Trafficking in Human Beings On November 2-3, 2026, a two-day regional workshop titled "Preventing Human Trafficking and Labour Exploitation in Tourism and Hospitality Supply Chains in Central Asia," was organised in Tashkent. Representatives from government agencies, international organizations, the tourism and hospitality industries, and civil society from Central Asian countries gathered to discuss practical measures to prevent human trafficking and labour exploitation in tourism and hospitality supply chains. The workshop focused on practical measures to combat trafficking in human beings and labour exploitation, strengthen the protection of workers and children, and promote responsible business practices across the tourism and hospitality sectors. Participants discussed national approaches to preventing human trafficking and labour exploitation in Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, and Tajikistan. In their presentations state officials highlighted the importance of effective labour inspection, law enforcement, interagency co-operation, and compliance with labour legislations. International experts also shared their perspectives on human rights due diligence in business operations, responsible tourism, and the protection of workers in vulnerable situations, as well as the implementation of child safeguarding and protection measures in tourism and hospitality services and close coordination with civil society. “Guests should be able to trust that the people cleaning their rooms and preparing their meals are treated fairly,” said Ambassador Antti Karttunen, OSCE Project Co-ordinator in Uzbekistan. “Protecting people is also an investment in tourism, a sector that creates jobs and supports the country’s economy.” As Fabian Bonertz, Senior Adviser and Supply Chains Project Lead at the OSCE Office of the Special Representative and Co-ordinator for Combating Trafficking in Human Beings, noted, tourism growth must go hand in hand with the protection of workers’ rights: "By strengthening human rights due diligence, promoting responsible recruitment and improving co-operation across supply chains, we can help ensure that the benefits of tourism are not built on the exploitation of vulnerable workers." Participants developed recommendations to prevent human trafficking and labour exploitation in tourism and hospitality supply chains. Through group exercises and regional discussions, they identified ways to make supply chains more transparent and improve co-operation among authorities, businesses and civil society. The event was organized by the OSCE Office of the Special Representative and Co-ordinator for Combating Trafficking in Human Beings (OSR/CTHB) in close co-operation with the OSCE Project Co-ordinator in Uzbekistan and in partnership with the National Commission on Combating Human Trafficking and Decent Work, with the support of the OSCE Programme Office in Astana, the OSCE Programme Office in Bishkek, the OSCE Programme Office in Dushanbe, and the Embassy of Germany in Uzbekistan. https://dushanbe.osce.org/news/programme.body: News News Item The OSCE supports law enforcement agencies from Tajikistan in enhancing their theoretical knowledge and practical skills in fighting cybercrime From 25 to 30 October 2026, the OSCE Programme Office in Dushanbe facilitated the participation of five officers from the Ministry of Internal Affairs (MIA) and four prosecutors from the General Prosecutor’s Office (GPO) in a five-day practical learning course on Digital Forensics and Open-Source Intelligence in Countering Cybercrime. The course was held at the Law Enforcement Academy of Uzbekistan in Tashkent, in co-operation with the OSCE Project Co-ordinator in Tashkent. Issued on: 4 November 2026 Issued by: OSCE Programme Office in Dushanbe Fields of work: Policing From 25 to 30 October 2026, the OSCE Programme Office in Dushanbe facilitated the participation of five officers from the Ministry of Internal Affairs (MIA) and four prosecutors from the General Prosecutor’s Office (GPO) in a five-day practical learning course on Digital Forensics and Open-Source Intelligence in Countering Cybercrime. The course was held at the Law Enforcement Academy of Uzbekistan in Tashkent, in co-operation with the OSCE Project Co-ordinator in Tashkent. Participants from the MIA and the GPO were selected based on their active participation and performance during previously conducted basic learning courses organized by experts from the Law Enforcement Academy in Dushanbe in April and August 2026. The advanced on-site course aimed to build on participants’ theoretical knowledge and improve their practical skills in combating cybercrime. During the learning course, participants had the opportunity to exchange experiences and learn about advanced methods of digital forensics, the legal regulation of digital evidence, and techniques for gathering information from open sources. Other topics included blockchain technology analysis, the role of the KODEX digital platform in cybercrime investigations, forensic examination of the darknet, and mechanisms for international co-operation in cybercrime investigations. Participants from Tajikistan pose for a group photo in front of the Law Enforcement Academy of Uzbekistan, where the advanced training course took place, Tashkent, 30 October 2026. This initiative, which included both basic and advanced practical learning courses, aimed to equip participants with the knowledge and skills needed for effective cybercrime intelligence gathering and investigations, while incorporating international best practices into their work. https://astana.osce.org/news/programme-o.body: News News Item Kazakhstan strengthens its capacity to combat cybercrime through implementation of National Cybercrime Training Framework Issued on: 4 November 2026 Issued by: OSCE Programme Office in Astana As digital technologies continue to transform criminal activity, the ability of law enforcement officers to identify, collect, preserve, and properly handle digital evidence has become increasingly important for effective investigations. To address this need, the OSCE Programme Office in Astana supported the implementation of the National Cybercrime Training Framework for Law Enforcement and Judiciary (NCTF LEJ) through a series of training activities across Kazakhstan in September and October 2026. The initiative aimed to strengthen professional capacities of law enforcement agencies in addressing cybercrimes by providing law enforcement educational institutions with a training package, “Handling Digital Evidence During Investigative Actions” (Basic Level). The pilot series followed a two-stage approach, combining the preparation of national trainers with the subsequent professional development of active-duty police officers. The first stage took place in September 2026 and focused on preparing the teaching staff of educational institutions of the Ministry of Interior (MoI) and other law enforcement agencies of the Republic of Kazakhstan through a Training of Trainers (ToT) programme. Three-day training sessions were held on 2-4 September at the MoI Management Academy in Astana, 7-9 September at the MoI Karaganda Academy, and 21-23 September at the MoI Almaty Academy. In addition to familiarizing participants with the course curriculum, the ToT programme equipped them with the methodological knowledge and practical tools required to independently deliver the training course. The sessions covered the legal framework and fundamental principles of handling electronic evidence, the management of digital crime scenes, and the documentation of investigative actions. Following the September ToT sessions, the newly prepared trainers put their knowledge into practice by delivering a series of professional development courses for active-duty police officers. The three-day courses took place on 7-9 October in Astana, 12-14 October in Karaganda and 27-29 October in Almaty, at the respective MoI educational institutions. The courses brought together first responders, general investigators, and other police personnel involved in handling digital evidence. Moving beyond theoretical knowledge, the training course focused on the practical challenges officers may encounter during investigative actions when handling digital evidence. Participants examined the legal admissibility of digital evidence, initial procedures at crime scenes, preparation for searches, and the specific considerations involved in handling various devices containing digital evidence. Practical sessions also addressed the proper packaging and labelling of electronic devices, documentation of searches and seizures, and photo and video recording at crime scenes. Through exercises, case studies, and practical scenarios, participants had the opportunity to apply the knowledge acquired throughout the course. Entry and final assessments were conducted to evaluate learning outcomes. The training activities in Astana also provided a platform for interagency participation. Both the ToT programme and the professional development course brought together representatives of Kazakhstan Court Administration, the Supreme Court of the Republic of Kazakhstan, the Law Enforcement Academy under the Prosecutor General's Office of Kazakhstan, the Academy of the National Security Committee, Aktobe, Almaty, Karaganda and Kostanay MoI Academies, and the MoI Management Academy in Astana. Throughout both stages, international and national experts of the OSCE Programme Office in Astana provided expert and methodological support. The completion of the Basic Level marks the first stage of a broader, phased training programme designed within NCTF LEJ to strengthen Kazakhstan's national capacity to combat cybercrime, enhance digital investigation capabilities and improve the handling of electronic evidence. The programme is envisaged to continue with Intermediate and Advanced Levels, providing opportunities for participants to progressively deepen their knowledge and develop more specialized practical competencies in handling digital evidence and conducting investigations involving digital technologies. The series was made possible through support from the governments of Finland, Germany, Norway, and the United Kingdom within the Office’s extrabudgetary project “Supporting the Republic of Kazakhstan in Developing Effective Policies on Countering Cybercrime”, implemented jointly with the Ministry of Interior and supported by the Presidential Administration of Kazakhstan since August 2023. https://odihr.osce.org/odihr/669435.body: Press release ODIHR stresses the importance of ensuring the independence, impartiality and effective functioning of Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal Date: 3 November 2026 Place: WARSAW Source: OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights WARSAW, 3 November – The OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR) is closely following recent developments regarding the Constitutional Tribunal of Poland, recalling the fundamental importance of ensuring the Tribunal’s independence, impartiality and effective functioning, in full accordance with the Polish Constitution, OSCE commitments and relevant international standards. In this context, ODIHR emphasizes that effective access to constitutional justice must be guaranteed both in law and in practice. Individuals should have a meaningful opportunity to seek protection of their constitutional rights and to obtain effective remedies. Any developments that undermine the Tribunal's ability to fulfil its constitutional mandate risk weakening these essential safeguards, undermining public trust in the institution and eroding the protection of human rights. Building on its longstanding engagement with the Polish authorities in addressing rule of law challenges, ODIHR wishes to underline the crucial importance of ensuring that any measures affecting the composition, independence or functioning of the Constitutional Tribunal are undertaken in accordance with international standards and with due regard for judicial independence, legal certainty and appropriate procedural safeguards. ODIHR remains ready to support Poland's efforts to strengthen judicial independence and the rule of law, through the provision of technical expertise and engagement in inclusive dialogue with relevant stakeholders. https://hcnm.osce.org/hcnm/669402.body: Press release “Efforts to uphold the rights and dignity of citizens are never in vain,” says 2026 Max van der Stoel Award winner Date: 2 November 2026 Place: THE HAGUE Source: OSCE High Commissioner on National Minorities THE HAGUE, 3 November 2026 – “Standing here today, I would like to send one clear message: efforts to uphold the rights and dignity of citizens are never in vain, particularly when they are directed towards those in minority communities,” said Lidija Županić Šuica, founder and director of Education for the 21st Century. She received the 2026 Max van der Stoel Award on behalf of Education for the 21st Century, an organization from Serbia at a ceremony at the Peace Palace in The Hague today, attended by representatives from governments, civil society and international organizations. Presenting the award on behalf of the Foreign Ministry of the Netherlands, Ambassador for International Organisations Erik Weststrate stated: “Education for the 21st Century helps close the gap between principles on paper and reality in the classroom. Their work ensures that minority rights are not just legal commitments, but lived experiences for the next generation. That is why the Netherlands is proud to present them with the Max van der Stoel Award.” Speaking on behalf of the jury, OSCE High Commissioner on National Minorities Christophe Kamp said: “Education for the 21st Century promotes the teaching of history as a process of critical reflection so that students can appreciate the diverse perspectives and historical narratives that exist in a multicultural society. [It] raises the visibility of national minorities, promotes inclusive historical narratives, and supports social cohesion across the region.” The Max van der Stoel Award – a prize of €50,000 – has been organized by the office of the High Commissioner on National Minorities and sponsored by the Dutch Foreign Ministry every two years since 2003. It is presented to a person, group or institution, in recognition of their extraordinary achievements in improving the position of national minorities across the OSCE area. Max van der Stoel was appointed as the first OSCE High Commissioner in 1992 and served eight and a half years in the post. He was twice Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Netherlands, and held seats in both the upper and lower houses of the Dutch Parliament. He served as Permanent Representative of the Netherlands to the United Nations and was awarded the honorary title of Minister of State by the then Queen Beatrix. Event material can be found here . Learn more about the winner here .
